# Gospel of Thomas — The HESED Reader's Guide
**Guide by:** HESED (חֶסֶד — Lovingkindness)

---

## At a Glance
| | |
|---|---|
| **Author** | Attributed to Didymus Judas Thomas (the apostle); anonymous actual authorship |
| **Date** | Core sayings possibly c. 50–70 CE; current form c. 100–140 CE |
| **Audience** | Likely a Syrian Christian community; possibly the "Thomas Christianity" of Edessa |
| **Genre** | Sayings gospel (logion collection) — no narrative, only 114 sayings of Jesus |
| **Timeline** | Possibly incorporating traditions as early as the Synoptic Gospels, in a very different form |
| **In One Sentence** | A collection of 114 sayings attributed to the living Jesus — discovered in 1945 in Egypt, written in Coptic — that offers a Jesus who speaks in riddles about inner light, the Kingdom within, and a salvation through self-knowledge rather than faith in his death and resurrection. |

---

## The World Behind the Text

In December 1945, near the Egyptian town of Nag Hammadi, a farmer named Muhammad Ali al-Samman was digging in the base of a cliff when he struck a large sealed clay jar. Fearing (or hoping) the jar contained a jinn, he hesitated before breaking it open. Inside he found twelve leather-bound papyrus codices containing texts in Coptic, the latest form of the ancient Egyptian language. Among them — as part of Codex II — was the Gospel of Thomas.

The text as we have it is a Coptic translation, probably made in the fourth century, of a Greek original that was composed probably in the early second century, drawing on a collection of Jesus traditions that may be even older. Fragments of three Greek versions of some Thomas sayings were already known from Oxyrhynchus papyri (discovered 1897, 1903) — small scraps found in the trash heaps of an ancient Egyptian town — but no one had realized they were from a gospel of Thomas until the Nag Hammadi discovery.

The world behind Thomas is Syrian Christianity. "Thomas" in Aramaic means "twin," and the full name — Didymus Judas Thomas — means "twin-twin" (both Greek didymos and Aramaic toma mean twin). The Thomas tradition (developed most fully in the Acts of Thomas and the Book of Thomas the Contender) identifies Thomas as the twin brother of Jesus. This is not a minor claim — it makes Thomas uniquely qualified to transmit Jesus's secret teachings, since he is, in some metaphysical sense, Jesus's double. The community that produced this gospel believed they had access to esoteric wisdom from the source.

---

## Why This Book Was Written

The Gospel of Thomas opens with a remarkable claim: "These are the secret sayings that the living Jesus spoke and Didymus Judas Thomas recorded." The key word is "secret" (Coptic: hēp; Greek: apokryphos, hidden). This gospel positions itself as the esoteric supplement to the public teachings — the private instruction that Jesus gave to his inner circle, as opposed to the parables he told the crowds. The purpose is to preserve and transmit this hidden wisdom to those capable of understanding it.

What is the content of this hidden wisdom? The Gospel of Thomas is not a systematic theology. Its 114 sayings range widely: some are close parallels to Synoptic sayings (the Parable of the Sower, the Lost Sheep, the Leaven), some are unique, some are familiar sayings in startlingly different forms, and some are deeply cryptic. The common thread, if there is one, is the primacy of inner knowledge — gnosis — as the path to salvation. The Kingdom of God in Thomas is not future and cosmic but present and interior: "The Kingdom of the Father is spread out upon the earth, and men do not see it" (saying 113). "If you know yourselves, then you will be known, and you will understand that you are children of the living Father" (saying 3).

The text was also written to preserve a Thomas community's theological identity against other streams of Christianity. The relationship between Thomas and the canonical Gospels is complex and debated: did Thomas preserve independent early traditions, or did it rework Synoptic material? Most scholars now see a two-way relationship — some Thomas sayings may genuinely represent independent early traditions (possibly even earlier than the Synoptic versions in some cases), while others clearly represent deliberate rewriting of Synoptic material in a more "Thomasine" or Gnosticizing direction.

---

## How to Read This Book

The Gospel of Thomas has no story. There is no baptism, no Galilean ministry, no passion narrative, no resurrection appearance. There is only: "Jesus said..." again and again, 114 times. Reading it requires a different posture than reading a narrative gospel — more like reading wisdom literature (Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, the Wisdom of Solomon) than like reading Mark.

Read it first in a single sitting to get the feel of the whole. Notice the range: some sayings will feel immediately familiar ("Whoever has will be given more; whoever does not have, even the little they have will be taken from them" — saying 41), some will feel like intriguing variations on familiar material, and some will stop you completely.

The sayings worth pausing longest over include:

Saying 3: The Kingdom is inside you and outside you. Know yourself and you will be known. If you do not know yourself, you live in poverty — and you are poverty.

Saying 70: "If you bring forth what is within you, what you bring forth will save you. If you do not bring forth what is within you, what you do not bring forth will destroy you." This is one of the most psychologically powerful statements in early Christian literature.

Saying 77: "I am the light that is over all things. I am all: from me all came forth, and to me all attained. Split a piece of wood; I am there. Lift up the stone, and you will find me there." This saying — with its mystical claim that Christ is present in the material world in every act of labor and every turned stone — is simultaneously the most beautiful and most theologically complex in the collection.

Saying 114 is the most controversial. Simon Peter says: "Let Mary leave us, for women are not worthy of life." Jesus replies: "Look, I will guide her to make her male, so that she too may become a living spirit resembling you males. For every female who makes herself male will enter the kingdom of heaven." This saying has generated enormous discussion. It may reflect an ascetic tradition in which "becoming male" means transcending bodily/sexual existence; it may reflect a genuine tradition of the male disciples' resistance to Mary's leadership; it may be a late Gnostic addition. Whatever its origin, it stands as the last word of the gospel and demands interpretation.

---

## The Threads — How This Book Connects

The relationship between Thomas and the Synoptic Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke) is one of the most actively debated questions in New Testament scholarship. A minority of scholars (including Helmut Koester and Stephen Patterson) argue that Thomas preserves a sayings source that is independent of and possibly earlier than Q (the hypothetical source behind Matthew and Luke's shared material). If so, Thomas's versions of some sayings may represent the earliest recoverable form of Jesus's teaching. The majority view holds that Thomas's versions are reworkings of Synoptic material, but even in this view, the reworkings reveal fascinating theological priorities.

Saying 77 ("Split wood; I am there") connects to the Wisdom of Solomon's concept of Sophia/Wisdom permeating all creation (Wisdom 7:24–27) and to the Logos theology of John 1 ("through him all things were made"). Thomas's Christology is in some ways more cosmic than the Synoptics, less interested in Jesus's historical life and more interested in the pre-existent, pervasive Christ.

The conflict between Peter and Mary in sayings 21, 61, and 114 connects to the Gospel of Mary, where the same conflict appears with much greater narrative development. Both texts reflect a tradition of tension within early Christianity over the role of women, and specifically over Mary Magdalene's authority as recipient of private revelations from the risen Jesus.

The self-knowledge emphasis connects Thomas to the Delphic oracle ("know thyself"), to Stoic and Platonic philosophy, and to the broader Gnostic tradition. But Thomas's self-knowledge is not the Greek philosophical project of understanding one's rational nature — it is the recognition that one is a "child of the living Father," that one's true origin is divine, and that the ordinary world of matter and social identity is not one's true home.

---

## What a Modern Reader Might Miss

The most important thing to understand about Thomas is that it has no soteriology of the cross. Jesus never mentions his death as saving anyone. There is no last supper, no Gethsemane, no crucifixion, no resurrection. Salvation in Thomas comes through finding the correct interpretation of Jesus's sayings: "Whoever discovers the interpretation of these sayings will not taste death" (saying 1). This is a salvation through understanding — through illuminated consciousness — not through atonement.

This creates a fascinating contrast with Paul, for whom the cross is the center of everything ("I resolved to know nothing while I was with you except Jesus Christ and him crucified," 1 Cor 2:2). Paul and Thomas represent genuinely different Christianities, both claiming to transmit the authentic teaching of Jesus. The canon selected Paul's approach, but Thomas's approach was clearly alive and influential for at least the first three centuries of Christianity.

The form of the text — a sayings collection with no narrative frame — is also significant. Modern readers assume "gospel" means a story about Jesus. The word euangelion (gospel) just means "good news," and the Gospel of Thomas uses it to describe a collection of sayings. The Q source (which Matthew and Luke both used) was probably also a sayings collection without narrative. Thomas shows us what that genre looked like.

---

## Why This Book Isn't in Your Bible

The Gospel of Thomas was not included in the canon because it failed on the key criteria of proto-orthodox canonicity: it was not apostolic in the way required (the Thomas authorship claim was never widely accepted), it was not universally used across the major Christian centers, and its theology — particularly its lack of a passion narrative and its emphasis on esoteric knowledge over faith — was incompatible with the emerging orthodox synthesis.

Origen knew of a Gospel of Thomas and dismissed it. Hippolytus and Eusebius mention it disparagingly. By the fourth century, when canonical decisions were being made, the text was firmly associated with Gnostic or heterodox Christianity and excluded accordingly.

The 1945 discovery transformed scholarship. Before Nag Hammadi, Thomas was known only from a few Greek fragments and hostile references in the church fathers. The complete Coptic text revealed an extraordinarily rich and complex document that has permanently changed how scholars understand Christian origins. Today Thomas is arguably the most studied non-canonical gospel, and debates about its date and relationship to the Synoptics continue to generate vigorous scholarship.

---

## Timeline

| Date | Event |
|------|-------|
| c. 50–70 CE | Possible earliest layer of Thomas sayings (disputed) |
| c. 100–140 CE | Gospel of Thomas in approximately its current form |
| c. 150–200 CE | Greek manuscripts being copied (the Oxyrhynchus fragments) |
| c. 200 CE | Origen mentions and dismisses a Gospel of Thomas |
| c. 300 CE | Hippolytus and others associate Thomas with Gnostic Christianity |
| c. 340–360 CE | Coptic translation made; included in Nag Hammadi Codex II |
| 1897, 1903 CE | Oxyrhynchus papyrus fragments (P.Oxy. 1, 654, 655) published; not yet identified as Thomas |
| December 1945 CE | Nag Hammadi library discovered near Jabal al-Tarif, Egypt |
| 1959 CE | Full Coptic Thomas published |
| 1977 CE | Critical edition; ongoing scholarly debate about date and provenance |

---

*— HESED, Reader's Guide Division*
